pins.title: Change them
pins.sub: Damp socks steal heat and rub blisters. Carry a dry pair in a bag and swap at the next break. Merino still feels warm when it gets damp.

pins.kicker: Cotton socks on a cold hike?
pins.title: Switch to merino
pins.sub: Cotton soaks up sweat and turns cold. Ours are 80% merino with a cushioned sole, crew height, sold as 1 pair.

pins.title: Cleats on first
items: Put them on before the ice, not on it
Toe in first, then stretch over the heel
Check the chains sit flat under the sole
Take them off on bare rock and pavement
Steep ice or glacier? That needs crampons

pins.title: Pack traction
pins.sub: Shaded bends can stay icy all day, even when the trailhead is dry. Chain ice cleats stretch over your boots and roll up small enough to carry all winter.

pins.title: Check first
items: Reservations and camping still cost extra
Look up road and trail closures
Plan to be back before dark
pins.sub: See the guides: Smokies, Utah and Yellowstone.

pins.title: Wear gaiters
pins.sub: Snow melts inside your boots and soaks your socks. Leg gaiters strap under the sole and cover you from boot top to mid-calf.

pins.title: Don't forget
items: A warm layer and a rain shell
A headlamp, even for a short hike
More water and snacks than you think
An offline map on your phone
pins.sub: Free printable checklist: tap the pin.

pins.title: Snack every hour
pins.sub: Your body makes heat from food. Eat a little on a cold hike before you feel chilled, and pull on a warm layer the moment you stop. See the guide: 22 pages of winter tips and checklists.

pins.title: Log them
pins.sub: A printable mini trail journal: one sheet, three folds and one cut make an 8-page booklet that fits a shirt pocket.

pins.title: Know the steps
pins.sub: A printable emergency checklist: the kit for your pack, a two-minute check before every trip, and clear steps if you get lost or someone is hurt.
